concepts.title: Very Short Talks (2 -- 10 minutes)
concepts.one_liner: Short talks are often advertisements, designed to persuade the listener to read your paper, or to listen to a longer version of the talk.
concepts.content:
Short talks are often advertisements, designed to persuade the listener to read your paper, or to listen to a longer version of the talk. Rather than trying to convey many details about your work, you should aim to have the audience remember the main idea behind your work, and to share your excitement about the work.

For five minute talks describing students' final project class presentations, we suggest that the students cover these points:

1.  What problem did you address?

2.  Why is it interesting?

3.  Why is it hard?

4.  What was the key to your approach?

5.  How well did it work?

That structure can be used for other short talks, too. For very short

concepts.recap_md:

- Focus on the main idea and your enthusiasm.
- Cover problem, interest, difficulty, approach, and results in about five minutes.

concepts.title: Preparation
concepts.one_liner: We believe the keys to both a good talk and to overcoming nerves are the same: prepare and practice.
concepts.content:
(see figure: The key to a good talk: preparation and practice.)

We believe the keys to both a good talk and to overcoming nerves are the same: prepare and practice. Think through your talk. It's almost always better to give a talk from notes than to read it from a script--the audience feels you're speaking to them so it's easier for them to pay attention. But for people giving a talk in a language that they are not comfortable with, writing out a script ahead of time may be a better solution. There may be parts of the talk that you feel are difficult to get through. For those parts, even for a native speaker, it may help to write out what you plan to say. When you give the talk, you may ignore the script, but having written it out once will make it easier to say.

Think through the talk and find the story--how one part relates to the next. If you can't find that story, you may want to reorder the presentation to create a good story.

When you can, you should visit the room you'll be speaking in to identify any issues that may come up. Will you be blocking anyone as you stand at the lectern to give the talk? Will there be someone there to help you set up? You should decide how to position yourself so that you can see your presentation, and also engage well with the audience.
concepts.motivation_md: Preparation and practice help deliver a clear, engaging talk and reduce nervousness by familiarizing you with your material and environment.
concepts.recap_md:
- Prepare and practice to improve your talk and reduce nerves.
- Use notes rather than a script unless language comfort is an issue.
- Visit the speaking room beforehand to plan your setup and engagement.

concepts.title: Nervousness
concepts.one_liner: A great cure for nervousness is to practice the talk aloud.
concepts.content:
One of us writes, "I used to be a nervous public speaker. I still find the hours before giving a presentation to be stressful. I'm always reviewing my talk to try to improve it or to track down the answers to questions I think someone might ask me. The more I prepare, and the better I know the lecture material, the less stressed I am."

A great cure for nervousness is to practice the talk aloud. Practice by yourself. Practice in front of your friends.

One approach @Hoogterp to calming nervousness is to remind yourself, "Get over it. They're not there to see you, they're there to hear the information. Just convey the information to them."

Some find this quote, attributed to Dr. Rob Gilbert @Gilbert, to be helpful: "It's all right to have butterflies in your stomach. Your job is to get them to fly in formation."
concepts.motivation_md: Nervousness can hinder public speaking, but practicing aloud and adopting calming mental strategies help speakers gain confidence and focus on conveying information.
concepts.recap_md:
- Nervousness is common but decreases with preparation.
- Practice aloud alone and with friends to build confidence.
- Use mental reminders to focus on sharing information, not on yourself.

concepts.title: Your Distracted Audience
concepts.one_liner: Before giving a talk, your mental image of the audience may be of many people, listening to your every word.
concepts.content: Before giving a talk, your mental image of the audience may be of many people, listening to your every word. In reality, on most every speaking situation, your audience is a collection of people who are checking their social media or email, looking on their laptops for other talks to attend, or are hungry or fidgety. How does one speak to such an audience? We have to practise and prepare in order to engage the audience.
concepts.motivation_md: Speakers must recognize that audiences are often distracted and prepare strategies to engage them effectively during talks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Audiences are often distracted by devices or other concerns.
- Expect less than full attention during talks.
- Practice and preparation help engage distracted listeners.

concepts.title: Ways to Engage the Audience
concepts.one_liner: The answer, of course, is to ask them questions.
concepts.content:
In the middle of Patrick Winston's talk about public speaking @WinstonSpeaks, he asks the audience the question, "Can you think of a technique to get the audience more engaged in the talk?" The answer, of course, is to ask them questions.

Bill Hoogterp @Hoogterp expands on that: "The audience is like a sheep dog, always wanting to be working. Give the audience something to work on while they're listening to you. 'Four' pushes people back, while 'two plus two' draws them in." You might pose a sub-problem to them that you had to address in your work, to get them thinking about how to solve that problem. Then they'll be more receptive to hear your solution.
concepts.motivation_md: Engaging the audience by asking questions keeps them mentally active and attentive during a talk.
concepts.recap_md:
- Asking questions is an effective way to engage the audience.
- Give the audience something to think about while listening.
- Pose sub-problems to draw listeners into your presentation.

concepts.title: Layer Your Talk
concepts.one_liner: It's often easier for the audience to listen to your talk if you layer it—provide verbal cues for new concepts and transitions between sections of the talk.
concepts.content:
### Layer Your Talk

It's often easier for the audience to listen to your talk if you layer it---provide verbal cues for new concepts and transitions between sections of the talk. This helps even the attentive listener to follow the structure of your talk. It keeps the distracted listener from being completely lost. The distracted listener, only listening for the verbal headings of your talk, may hear, "The probability of an observation has three terms to it. $ blah blah blah blah $ So that gives us the objective function we want to optimize. Now, how do we find the optimal value? There are two approaches you can take. $ blah blah blah blah So now, with these tools in hand, we can apply this methods to real images. $ blah blah blah blah $" Your verbal cues can help even a distracted listener follow your main points.

You can also make your talk easier to follow if you add verbal dynamics---variations in speed or intensity. Find a part of the talk that is particularly special to you and let that show through. One of us writes, "When I gave talks about image deblurring, I would emphasize one aspect that I particularly enjoy: 'I love this problem; it's beautifully underdetermined. There are many ways we can explain a blurry image. It could be that that's what was there in the world--- we took a sharp picture of a world that happened to look blurry. Or we took a blurred image of a sharp world.' " The audience loves to watch you be excited about something!
concepts.motivation_md: Layering your talk with verbal cues and dynamics helps all listeners follow your main points, especially those who are distracted.
concepts.recap_md:
- Use verbal cues to signal new concepts and transitions.
- Layering helps both attentive and distracted listeners.
- Add verbal dynamics to convey your enthusiasm.

concepts.title: People Like to See a Good Fight
concepts.one_liner: The audience loves to watch a good fight.
concepts.content:
As described by @Adelson95, the audience loves to watch a good fight. You can set up a fight between two competing conjectures. For example, you might say, "The flat earth theory predicts that ships will appear on the horizon as small versions of the complete ship. Under that theory, you’d expect approaching ships to appear as in @fig-boats-a. Conversely, the round earth theory predicts that the top of the sails will appear first, then gradually the rest of the ship below it, resulting in approaching ships looking as in @fig-boats-b. The audience waits with anticipation as you show them the result from your experiment, @fig-boats-c, thus revealing the winning theory."


(see figure: The appearance of ships approaching a port, from the flat-earth theory.)

(see figure: Their appearance as predicted by the round-earth theory.)

(see figure: The experimental evidence: a photograph of ships approaching a port.)

Fig (a) The appearance of ships approaching a port, from the flat-earth theory. (b) Their appearance as predicted by the round-earth theory. (c) The experimental evidence: a photograph of ships approaching a port @mnsomero
concepts.motivation_md: Setting up a conflict between competing theories engages the audience by creating anticipation for the resolution.
concepts.recap_md:
- Audiences enjoy seeing a 'good fight' between competing ideas.
- Present contrasting predictions to build suspense.
- Reveal experimental evidence to show which theory wins.

concepts.title: Show Yourself to the Audience
concepts.one_liner: An audience wants a technical talk to make sense, teach a few things, and connect with the speaker's excitement for the topic.
concepts.content:
In a lovely video, the actor Alan Alda describes the importance of connecting with the audience in scientific presentations @AlanAlda. Alda noted the improvement in scientific speaking of volunteers after they engaged in improvisational theater exercises. After the exercises, the volunteers were primed to engage and connect with others, and their scientific talks sparkled.

Here's what we think an audience wants from a technical talk: (a) To have one part follow from another and make sense. (b) To learn a few things. (c) To connect with the speaker, to share their excitement for the topic. They want to watch you love something!
concepts.motivation_md: Connecting with the audience makes technical talks more engaging and effective, helping listeners follow the talk, learn, and share the speaker's enthusiasm. This improves communication and impact.
concepts.recap_md:

- They want to learn a few things during the talk.
- They want to connect with the speaker's excitement for the topic.

concepts.title: How to End the Talk
concepts.one_liner: Better to close a talk with "Thank you." so the audience knows when to applaud, then ask for questions.
concepts.content:
How should you end your talk? A common, but awkward, way is to end by asking, "Are there any questions?" The audience wants to clap at the end of a talk, but with that ending, they don't know whether to applaud or to ask a question, and they're likely to give only scattered applause @Adelson95. Better is to close with "Thank you." The audience then knows it's their time to applaud, and they will. Then you can ask for questions.

We note that Patrick Winston disagrees with ending a talk with "thank you" @WinstonSpeaks. He didn't like the implication that the audience was doing you some favor for attending your talk, and preferred to remind the audience of how he has kept his earlier promise to them regarding what they would learn after they listened to his talk.
concepts.motivation_md: Ending a talk clearly signals to the audience when to applaud and when to ask questions, avoiding awkward pauses and scattered applause.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ending with "Are there any questions?" can confuse the audience.
- Closing with "Thank you." signals the audience to applaud.
- Some prefer reminding the audience of the talk's promise instead of "thank you."

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Good writing involves lots of rewriting, and improving clarity before submission is often more valuable than last-minute result improvements.
concepts.content: The approaches to writing and editing described previously all take time: good writing involves lots of rewriting. We find that the last days before a paper submission deadline are often better spent improving the structure, presentation, and clarity of the paper than in trying to obtain last-minute improvements to the results.
concepts.motivation_md: Revising and clarifying writing before submission enhances paper quality more effectively than last-minute result tweaks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Good writing requires extensive rewriting.
- Final days before submission are best used to improve clarity and structure.
- Prioritize presentation over last-minute result changes.

concepts.title: Introduction
concepts.one_liner: Giving good talks is important and can greatly help your work's impact, much like a big serve helps in tennis.
concepts.content: Giving good talks is important for people who use the material of this book--for students, researchers, and engineers. One might think, "It is the work itself that really counts. Giving a talk about it is secondary." But the ability to give a good talk is like having a big serve in tennis---by itself, it doesn't win the game for you, but it sure helps. And the very best tennis players all have great serves. So we include in this chapter material that we have found helpful in giving talks.
concepts.motivation_md: Effective talks enhance the impact and communication of your work, complementing the quality of the research itself.
concepts.recap_md:
- Giving good talks is important for students, researchers, and engineers.
- A good talk enhances the impact of your work.
- Like a big serve in tennis, it helps but doesn't replace the work itself.

concepts.title: A Taxonomy of Talks
concepts.one_liner: Talks vary widely in length and audience familiarity, requiring inclusion of material accessible to both novices and experts.
concepts.content: There are different kinds of talks. Conference and workshop talks may range in length between 3 minutes for a "fast-forward" talk to 45 or 60 minutes for a keynote address. You may be one of many speakers, sometimes speaking in different rooms at the same time. Sometimes you will visit a university or company and speak in a special seminar. (Here @MITFacultyJobTalks2022 is a list of tips regarding faculty job talks from the MIT faculty.) It is very often the case that the audience will have a wide range of familiarity with the work and topic that you will present about. In a small seminar to a competing research group, there may be many people who are very familiar with your work. But even in such a small seminar, and especially to a larger group, there may be many people who don't know your area, nor perhaps not even your broad area. So you will to include material to let the uninitiated not be lost. Even people who are very familiar with the topic will appreciate hearing material they already understand presented clearly and well.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the types of talks and audience diversity helps tailor presentations to be clear and engaging for all listeners.
concepts.recap_md:

- Audiences often have mixed familiarity with your topic.
- Include material accessible to novices and clear to experts.

prereq.rationale: Preparation for talks logically requires understanding the importance of giving talks to motivate the need for preparation and practice.

Understanding ways to engage the audience requires first recognizing that the audience is often distracted, as described in 'Your Distracted Audience'. This context motivates the need for engagement techniques such as asking questions.

The technique of layering your talk is motivated by the reality that audiences are often distracted, as explained in 'Your Distracted Audience'. Layering helps keep even distracted listeners following the main points.

overlay.rationale: The technique 'Structure for short talks' formalizes the informal advice given in 'Very Short Talks (2 -- 10 minutes)' by providing a concrete structure to follow for such talks, as shown in the overlapping passage L31508-L31518.

The taxonomy of talks concept is topically related to the importance of giving talks, as it elaborates on different kinds of talks and their audience considerations, complementing the introduction about the importance of talks.
Both 'Layer Your Talk' and 'Ways to Engage the Audience' provide complementary strategies to maintain audience attention and engagement during a talk.
The idea of setting up a 'good fight' between competing conjectures is a specific method to engage the audience, related to the broader topic of ways to engage the audience.
Showing yourself to the audience to connect and share excitement complements the general strategies for engaging the audience discussed earlier.
How to end the talk effectively is related to engaging the audience throughout the presentation, including the conclusion.
